name: story-workflow
applies_when: The correctness claim is that something new works. The work adds behaviour, changes what the system does, or fixes a defect, and the validation that would show it works does not exist yet -- it has to be written as part of the work. Choose this when what you are asking for is judged by whether it does something it did not do before.
max_run_cost_usd_reason: Run totals across 23 runs, story-040 through story-062, summing total_cost_usd across every agent invocation in the harness logs: median $15.12, p90 $55.79, max $124.98. The largest legitimate run was story-053 at $67.88; story-048's $124.98 escalated. $90 sits above the first with a third of margin and below the second, so exactly one run in twenty-three would have stopped, and it is the one that escalated anyway. The principle behind all five numbers, which is what a later reader needs in order to tighten them correctly: a cap that would have fired on work we were glad to have is set too low. These are the first ceilings this deployment has run under, they fail by truncating an agent mid-work, and there is no cost.json corpus yet -- so they are set at clearly pathological rather than merely unusual, and tightened later against the record this story starts writing. The logs the figures came from are gitignored and reach no clone, so this string is the only place the derivation survives. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.

stages.name: tester
stages.max_execution_cost_usd_reason: Per invocation across 23 runs, story-040 through story-062: n=35, p50 $3.27, p90 $12.99, max $52.56. This one is the deliberate one. The tester's expensive invocations are story-053's single legitimate $52.56 conversion and four from story-048's failing run, and no cap distinguishes them, so $75 leaves the legitimate one alone while stopping a call at well past the worst ever seen. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.
stages.max_self_routes_reason: Three, where every other budget in this workflow is one. The tester is the stage most often asked to produce something it has not produced before -- a new rule, a new idiom, a new fixture shape -- and a stage learning what to produce is the stage most likely to fail mechanically on a first attempt and then again while correcting itself. One budget covers the dropped connection; the second covers the first correction landing incomplete. The third was added on 2026-09-03 out of story-101, which escalated having spent one budget on a genuine suite failure, one on a turn that repaired it and then left test-results.json unwritten, and met a load-sensitive flake in tests/test_command_transport.py with nothing left. Two of the three causes there cost the stage nothing in judgement and one of them was not about this story's work at all, which is the case a third budget is for. It is a hedge and not the fix: the budget spends the same whatever the cause, and that is filed as a-forgotten-artifact-costs-a-failure. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the budget.

The observed maxima, $19.07 and $18.99, were both story-059 and both caused by the verifier starting a full suite run it could not wait for, which prompts/verifier.md now prevents; its real distribution is likely tighter and $30 is generous on purpose. correction_pass.budget_reason: Two, raised from one after story-086. A pass corrects the locations its findings name, and the verification after it can find the same claim standing somewhere the first findings did not reach: story-086's budget went on an exclusivity claim in .harness/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, and the next verification found the same claim in a test docstring with nothing left to spend, so it shipped recorded and uncorrected. One budget covers the findings a verification raises; the second covers what correcting them reveals. This is a ceiling on how many times the words may be revisited and not a licence to keep going: a pass changes prose and never behaviour, so neither pass can move what any test asserts. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the budget.

implementation.when: the defect is in the code under test: behaviour the story asked for is missing, wrong, or incomplete, and the tests report it correctly

validation.when: the defect is in the tests themselves: a wrong, missing or fragile assertion, an assertion that cannot fail, or coverage that does not exercise what it claims

documentation.when: the defect is in the documentation itself: it describes behaviour the code does not have, names a file, module or symbol that does not exist, contradicts what the run's own artifacts record, or omits a change the story required be written down. Judge the document against the code as it now stands: a document that accurately describes wrong behaviour is an implementation defect, not a documentation one, and belongs to the category that owns the code
